sample.n_individuals: Over 2,000,000 individuals per period, approximately half of the Danish adult population; Table 3 reports 2,240,332 and 2,295,922 observations for the two 2004 reform periods and 2,097,862 and 2,240,833 for the two 2009–10 reform periods

construction_notes: Monetary units are deflated to 2019-levels using the implied wage indexes in the tax code; USD 1 ≈ DKK 6.8.

Individual marginal tax rates are not observed in the data and are imputed with a detailed tax simulator (similar to the NBER TAXSIM), extending Kleven and Schultz (2014); marginal tax rates are computed as the increase in total household taxes due to an incremental increase in labor income.
'Taxable income' in the empirical analysis is operationalised as personal income (PI in Table 1), the income concept subject to the tax change; it is not the legal concept of taxable income (TI).
'Broad income' is the taxable income measure before deductions, which primarily consist of employer administrated pension contributions.
The baseline outcome is the four-year change in log income; 2- and 3-year changes are considered in the Online Appendix.

The instrument is the predicted BETWEEN-income change in the log marginal net-of-tax rate, E(Δ ln τ^p_{it−k} | z_{it−k}), rather than the individual predicted change, so that identification comes only from between-income tax variation.
Initial income always refers to personal income and is measured in the first year of each four-year period (1999 and 2003 for the 2004 reform; 2004 and 2008 for the 2009–10 reform).
Income bin dummies: DKK 10,000 bins in Eqs. (12), (13) and (15); 50 initial-income bins in Eq. (11); a DKK 1,000 grid (1,250 dummies) as a robustness check.
The 2009–10 reform window is set to 2008–2012 to avoid the anticipation-driven shifting of income from 2009 to 2010 documented by Kreiner et al. (2016).
